newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish inflation drops, raising hopes of rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Spanish inflation drops, raising hopes of rate cut.

text.p: Spanish inflation fell sharply in January, fanning hopes the Bank of Spain will lower its official interest rate on Friday and improving the nation's chances of joining the launch of Europe's single currency.

Spain reported on Thursday that inflation dropped to a year-on-year rate of 2.9 percent in January from 3.2 percent in December, better than market expectations for a more modest decline to 3.0 percent.

The benign data increased talk the central bank could lower its key money market rate for the second time this year at its regular repurchase tender on Friday, although nine of 15 analysts polled by Reuters still expected it to wait.
For Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato the data showed that the governments' work to whip the economy into shape for Europe's single currency was paying off.

"This is a historic number," he said. The progress in the fight against inflation "puts us clearly on the path to European monetary integration...The goal that once seemed impossible is now within reach."

The conservative Popular Party government has worked hard to reign in the deficit and debt, promote a stable peseta, and bring long-term rates and inflation down to fulfill the economic requirements of the common currency.
For many, inflation had been Spain's thorniest task, but the drop beneath three percent has gained the once notoriously bloated figure new respectability.
"It is a good number," said Valentin Fernandez, chief economist of Credit Lyonnais in Madrid. "The number confirms that this year we will have European inflation."

"One-tenth better than what was being forecast means that the market is divided 50 percent between those that believe the Bank if going to cut and 50 percent that believes it will not do, principally, to the recent episodes that have affected the peseta."

For a minority, it meant the Bank of Spain would sanction the second cut in its six percent money market interest rate this year. It shaved 25 basis points off the rate on January 16, bringing it down from nine percent at the start of last year.

"Inflation will raise expectations of an easing. We continue to forecast the Bank of Spain will cut rates by 50 basis points tomorrow," said Juan Antonio Mielgo, economist at the Bank of America in Madrid.

The only main hitch, the others say, is the peseta's recent volatility, which the Bank of Spain will certainly want to discourage. The central bank may also be more cautious as it looks ahead to a less tame inflation trend in 1998.
The peseta weakened beyond 85.00 per mark in January after months of holding steady near 84.00. At 1300 GMT, it was trading at 84.69/70.
